topics.topic: First-release procedure for finding and completing reviews of due customers and archived projects, including missing governance schedules
questions: What exact first-release actions let the owner find every customer and archived project due for review, what information do they show, and how does the owner know the review is complete or has failed?

What exact first-release procedure, inputs and observable result let the owner identify every customer and archived project due for action, and what happens if the governance schedule is still draft, missing or ambiguous?

quotes:
GDPR asks that retention periods be set, documented and kept (Art. 5(1)(e),
Art. 30, Recital 39); it does not ask Registry to count them. The periods —
the owner's provisional ones of R0-40 among them, to be checked against
accounting, tax, claim and building-warranty periods — are the governance's
retention schedule, applied by the owner's periodic review (once a year, say).
Registry gives that review what it needs and nothing more:

- the date a project was archived, and the owner's mark that a customer
  relationship has ended (R0-49), which the owner may clear (R0-57);

It holds neither the counters of R0-97 nor the review page of
R0-94. Until the second release the owner meets the review's purpose by
hand, from the governance's schedule.
judgement.why: The exact manual review procedure, its completion record and the response to a missing or ambiguous governance schedule are operational governance notes for State 7, while State 0 already names the Registry facts and actions available to that procedure.

topics.topic: Infrastructure observation, retained request or connection data, retention periods, and owner access
questions: Which infrastructure component observes ordinary HTTPS, what request metadata or security events does it retain, for how long, and what—if anything—the owner can inspect in the first release?
Which infrastructure components exist, what request or connection facts each observes or records, how long those facts remain, and whether any of them are available to the owner?

quotes:
Ordinary reads, agent calls and the inner steps of flows
are not recorded in Registry; security events of the infrastructure are
handled by the infrastructure, outside Registry.

The signs of an attempt that only
Registry tells apart — a sign-in lockout, a call with a token Registry does not
know, a token asking beyond its rights, Kernel's calls outside a session's
set — stay unseen by the owner until then: Registry refuses them and keeps no
trace (A13 rule 3, A14 rule 2), and the infrastructure, to which they are
ordinary HTTPS, sees only what it sees of its own.

Deploying Registry, its release process and the host's administration (vNext
§15). Registry does not manage deployment.
judgement.why: Infrastructure logging components, retained metadata, retention periods and operator access are deployment and operational notes outside Registry's State 0 product behavior.

topics.topic: When the first-release workaround and accepted visibility gap end
questions: Does the first-release workaround and accepted visibility gap end when the second release's specification change starts, when that release is admitted, or when it is deployed to production?

quotes:
It holds neither the counters of R0-97 nor the review page of
R0-94. Until the second release the owner meets the review's purpose by
hand, from the governance's schedule.

Deploying Registry, its release process and the host's administration (vNext
§15). Registry does not manage deployment.
judgement.why: The text fixes when design work on the second change starts and what that release must contain, but the production handover that ends an interim operating procedure belongs to the excluded release and deployment process recorded in State 7 notes.

topics.topic: Whether closing attempts remain visible across process lifetimes until the owner signs in
questions: Does “closing” promise that the owner will eventually see every counted attempt, or only attempts still present in the current process lifetime when the owner next signs in?

quotes:
In the second release (R0-100), Registry counts refused attempts in memory
from its start and
shows them to the owner on the first page after sign-in, with the instant of
the start and of the latest of each kind: refused sign-ins and lockouts;
calls on the service API with a token Registry does not know; calls whose
token does not allow the operation or class asked; and, apart from these,
Kernel's agent-authority calls refused for a session or a project outside
its set, the weakest sign, since a revocation by the owner yields them too.
The counters hold no value, no credential, no address and no request; a
restart clears them, as it clears the lockout. The audit log stays a record
of accepted changes (R0-58).
judgement.why: The promise is explicitly best-effort visibility within the current process lifetime, because the counters start with the process and a restart clears them.

topics.topic: Which additional failed or contextless operations are covered by the accepted first-release visibility gap
questions: Is this list exhaustive, or does the owner's accepted first-release gap also cover ordinary refused sign-ins, calls naming an unregistered session, and project operations with neither a named nor an active project?

quotes:
In the second release (R0-100), Registry counts refused attempts in memory
from its start and
shows them to the owner on the first page after sign-in, with the instant of
the start and of the latest of each kind: refused sign-ins and lockouts;
calls on the service API with a token Registry does not know; calls whose
token does not allow the operation or class asked; and, apart from these,
Kernel's agent-authority calls refused for a session or a project outside
its set, the weakest sign, since a revocation by the owner yields them too.

A call naming a
session that is not registered is refused like a call outside the set (R0-47),
an access request included; registering a session already registered returns
it unchanged (round 6 T2).

It holds neither the counters of R0-97 nor the review page of
R0-94. Until the second release the owner meets the review's purpose by
hand, from the governance's schedule. The signs of an attempt that only
Registry tells apart — a sign-in lockout, a call with a token Registry does not
know, a token asking beyond its rights, Kernel's calls outside a session's
set — stay unseen by the owner until then: Registry refuses them and keeps no
trace (A13 rule 3, A14 rule 2), and the infrastructure, to which they are
ordinary HTTPS, sees only what it sees of its own.
judgement.why: Ordinary refused sign-ins are explicitly counted, while an unregistered session and a contextless project call are explicitly answered as outside-set calls, placing all three within the refusal categories that remain unseen in the first release.
